title: Meatballs
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Kane reflects on teaching Dan Meyer's Meatballs three-act task as a full class period for the first time, rather than a twenty-minute insert. He describes the sequence: written estimates before discussion to avoid anchoring, identifying needed information, an analysis assignment on assumptions and measurement choices, then the reveal in which only two of his eighth graders got the right answer. His wins were divergent thinking and real investment in the third act. His losses were weak accounts of sources of error and a flopped extension, which showed students' belief that a wrong answer must be a calculation mistake. It is a candid teacher reflection with a concrete plan to facilitate the error conversation as a group next time.
points: Having students record guesses before sharing minimizes anchoring on other students' estimates.
Students were uncomfortable that the radius had no single right answer, but most soon dove in, producing divergent thinking.
The analysis assignment on assumptions and chosen values pushed students to justify their method, not just compute.
Students tended to blame a calculation mistake whenever the answer was off, exposing a weak sense of modeling error.
Next time Kane plans to facilitate the sources-of-error discussion as a group to give students footholds.
quotes: I taught Dan Meyer's Meatballs 3-act task this week. It was the first time I've spent an entire class on a 3-act, rather than inserting it into an objective and spending 20 minutes on a task that fits into my curriculum more neatly. I really enjoyed it, and many of my students did as well, although there was definitely some frustration.

I opened with the first act, and had students make an estimate of many meatballs it would take to make the pot overflow, as well as guesses they thought were too high and too low. I've found it critical here to have students write down their guesses first, to minimize the effect of initial guesses anchoring other students' ideas. Then, students wrote down what information they needed in order to answer the question and laid out their path to a solution.

Once students found an answer, I gave them an analysis assignment. They had to neatly recreate they key steps of their work (they had calculators to use), describe their solution method name the assumptions they made in their solution method, and describe why they chose the values they used for the various measurements.
Only 2 of my 8th graders got it right. Then, they worked through the rest of their analysis, considering sources of error and how they caused the difference between their calculation and the answer.

Lots of kids freaked out a little bit when I told them there was no "right answer" for the radius, but after initial hesitation I was excited about how many kids dove right in Investment. Kids wanted to get the right answer, and were really engaged in the third act.

I didn't get many high-quality answers for sources of error--too many kids just said they made a mistake in their calculation, or provided an error that would make the answer too small when theirs was too large/vice versa. Next time I want to work on facilitating more of that conversation as a group to give students footholds into different sources of error

The extension question was a flop. Very few kids figured out it was because there's space between baseballs in a bucket, and again kids were saying "he made a mistake in the calculation" ... showing their tendency to believe that an answer that isn't "right" must be a calculation error.
